_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss in another section (Tom's children vs Marcus's worries; Leila's lonely winter vs Hannah's cool neighbours). Used by the Part 7 practice page.
title: A change of scenery
subtitle: Four people describe moving between the city and the countryside.

sections.A: Hannah, 34, graphic designer. I'd loved my ten years in Manchester, but after a long illness I wanted somewhere quiet to get my strength back. My partner and I ended up in an old stone farmhouse at the end of a track in mid-Wales, three miles from the nearest shop. I'd assumed working from home would be simple, but the broadband turned out to be hopeless. For the first six months, whenever I had to send a large file to a client, I drove to the top of the hill behind the house, where the signal was stronger, and sat in the car with my laptop on the steering wheel. The neighbours were polite but distant at first. I was never lonely, though; there was too much to do. Things changed the spring I spent a fortnight helping the farmer next door with his lambs at three in the morning. Now I'm invited to everything.
sections.B: Tom, 67, retired postman. I spent forty years delivering letters around the villages of Aberdeenshire, so when I told my son and daughter I was selling the cottage and buying a flat in the middle of Glasgow, they both said I'd lost my mind. My wife had died two years before, and the cottage felt far too big and far too silent. Now I can walk to the cinema, the library and three different cafés in under ten minutes, and I sold my old estate car last spring because it hadn't left its parking space for months. The first few weeks were hard, I'll admit. Buses, sirens and people chatting on the pavement at two in the morning kept me awake night after night. These days, oddly, the sound of the street outside helps me drop off. It tells me I'm not on my own, and I find that a comfort.
sections.C: Leila, 28, nurse. Honestly, it was about money. On a nurse's salary in London I was sharing a flat with three strangers and paying a fortune for a room barely bigger than my bed. In a small town in North Yorkshire, I could rent a whole cottage with a garden for less. I got a job at the hospital in York, which means forty minutes each way on country roads, but I've come to enjoy that drive. What I hadn't prepared for was the first winter. It got dark at four, I didn't know a soul, and on my days off I sometimes went from morning to night without speaking to anyone. I remember ringing my mum and crying down the phone. Then a colleague persuaded me to join the community choir. I can't really sing, but nobody seems to mind, and half my friends here are altos.
sections.D: Marcus, 41, chef. My wife and I had run a busy restaurant in Bristol for years, and we were both exhausted. When a little place came up for sale in a fishing village in Cornwall, we went for it, though I lay awake for weeks worrying about our two boys. They were nine and eleven, used to football clubs and cinemas, and I was sure they'd be bored within a week. I couldn't have been more wrong. Their new school has thirty-two pupils, they spend every weekend on the beach, and the younger one can name more seabirds than I can name herbs. Business is crazy in August and very quiet in February, which took some getting used to. The biggest change in my cooking is that most of the vegetables on the menu now come from the field behind the restaurant, which I dig myself before breakfast.

questions.question: Which person was told by relatives that the decision was a foolish one?
questions.why: 'They both said I'd lost my mind.' Marcus worried about his sons, but nobody criticised the move.

questions.question: Which person had to find a way round a technical difficulty?
questions.why: The broadband was 'hopeless', so she 'drove to the top of the hill… where the signal was stronger'.

questions.question: Which person now finds reassuring something that once disturbed them?
questions.why: Street noise 'kept me awake', but now 'helps me drop off… I find that a comfort'.

questions.question: Which person moved mainly for financial reasons?
questions.why: 'Honestly, it was about money.' Hannah moved for her health, and Marcus because he was exhausted.

questions.question: Which person feared their children would not adapt to the new place?
questions.why: 'I was sure they'd be bored within a week.' Tom's children were adults who objected to the move, not ones who had to adapt.

questions.question: Which person felt cut off from other people for a while?
questions.why: 'I didn't know a soul… without speaking to anyone.' Hannah's neighbours were distant, but she says 'I was never lonely'.

questions.question: Which person won over the local community by lending a hand?
questions.why: After 'helping the farmer next door with his lambs… Now I'm invited to everything.'

questions.question: Which person no longer has a vehicle?
questions.why: 'I sold my old estate car last spring.' Leila still drives forty minutes each way.

questions.question: Which person produces some of the food they serve?
questions.why: 'Most of the vegetables on the menu now come from the field behind the restaurant, which I dig myself.'

questions.question: Which person was helped to settle in by joining a group activity?
questions.why: A colleague 'persuaded me to join the community choir… half my friends here are altos'.
